*   Understanding of voltage dividers.

## Introduction & background

To fix the $\beta$-dependency problem discovered yesterday, engineers use negative feedback, specifically "emitter degeneration." By adding a resistor to the emitter leg, the voltage gain of the amplifier is determined almost entirely by the ratio of the external resistors ($R_C / R_E$) rather than the transistor's internal $\beta$. 
The second circuit, a current mirror, is a clever way to copy a specific current to another part of a circuit. It relies on the fact that two identical transistors manufactured together (or at least of the same part number) will pull the same collector current if they are forced to share the exact same base-emitter voltage ($V_{BE}$).

## Core equations

Common Emitter Voltage Gain (with emitter degeneration):
$$A_v \approx -\frac{R_C}{R_E}$$

Current mirror constraint:
$$V_{BE1} = V_{BE2} \implies I_{C1} \approx I_{C2}$$

## Diagram

[Wikipedia: Basic BJT Current Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_mirror)

## What you're building

1. A $\beta$-independent common-emitter amplifier using emitter degeneration.
2. A two-transistor current mirror biased to provide a steady 1 mA reference current.
3. A test setup to measure how reliably the mirror copies that 1 mA current into varying load resistors.

## Activity

Breadboard a common-emitter amp: 2N3904, Rc = 4.7 kΩ, Re = 470 Ω, bias divider 47 k/10 k from 9 V; AC-couple 100 mV @ 1 kHz in; measure gain. Then breadboard a 2-transistor current mirror with a 1 mA reference; measure the copied current into 2–3 different load resistors.

## Question to answer

1. Does the amp's gain land near $-R_C/R_E = -10$ — and why did $\beta$ vanish from the result?
2. Why does shorting the mirror's Q1 collector to its base force exactly the right $V_{BE}$ to copy the current?

## Additional resources

*   Fronczak II, the basic current-mirror question (his note: "the answer is clearly 1 mA").
*   Fronczak II temperature question: $V_{BE}$ drifts $\approx -2 \text{ mV}/^\circ\text{C}$, so which way does the mirror's output drift?
